prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a class cannot be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) where individual damages questions will overwhelm common questions.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Individualized Damages Questions Overwhelm Any Common Questions, So Rule 23(b)(3) Predominance Is Not Satisfied.**

Rule 23(b)(3) permits a class action only if "questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members." Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3). Predominance is "far more demanding" than Rule 23(a)'s commonality requirement. The plaintiff bears the burden of proving it by a preponderance of the evidence. *See Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 811, 815 (7th Cir. 2012). The inquiry asks whether common issues are the important part of the case, and whether resolving them will advance the litigation. It does not ask whether a common question can be identified somewhere in the dispute. *See id.* at 815; *Pella Corp. v. Saltzman*, 606 F.3d 391, 394 (7th Cir. 2010). Courts must also look past the pleadings to how the case would actually be tried. *Oshana v. Coca-Cola Co.*, 472 F.3d 506, 513 (7th Cir. 2006).

**A. A damages model must match the plaintiffs' theory of liability and be capable of classwide proof.**

The Supreme Court has held that a damages model must measure only damages attributable to the plaintiff's theory of liability. A model that cannot do so cannot establish predominance. *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 35 (2013). This Court applies *Comcast* to reject certification when plaintiffs cannot show that damages can be proven on a common basis. *See Suchanek v. Sturm Foods, Inc.*, 764 F.3d 750, 760 (7th Cir. 2014). Plaintiffs' proposed method does not meet that standard. It assumes that every class member suffered the same injury and lost the same amount. The record shows otherwise. [Insert record cites: variation in purchase circumstances, use, price paid, and mitigation.]

**B. The individualized inquiries here are the heart of the case, not an afterthought.**

Defendant acknowledges that "the need for individual damages determinations" does not by itself defeat certification. *See Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 801 (7th Cir. 2013); *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815. That principle assumes liability can be resolved on a classwide basis, leaving only the arithmetic of damages for later. Where that is so, damages issues can be handled separately. *See Butler*, 727 F.3d at 800–01. This case is different. Whether each class member was injured at all, and in what amount, depends on facts unique to that person. Those facts include what each person bought, what each knew when buying, and what each paid. Damages and injury are therefore not separable from liability. Resolving them would require a mini-trial for each class member. When the "individual" inquiries are the substantial part of the litigation, they predominate. *See Andrews v. Chevy Chase Bank*, 545 F.3d 570, 573–77 (7th Cir. 2008); *Oshana*, 472 F.3d at 514–15.

This Court has repeatedly refused to certify classes when the need to establish each member's entitlement would swamp any common issue. *See CE Design Ltd. v. King Architectural Metals, Inc.*, 637 F.3d 721, 724–26 (7th Cir. 2011) (affirming denial of certification where individualized inquiries into class members' circumstances outweighed common questions); *Pella*, 606 F.3d at 394 (reversing certification where individualized issues dominated). A common question that merely begins the analysis does not satisfy Rule 23(b)(3) when each member would still have to prove injury and damages through separate evidence. *Cf. Thorogood v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 547 F.3d 742, 747–48 (7th Cir. 2008) (explaining that predominance depends on what must be proved class member by class member).

**C. Case management tools cannot cure the defect.**

Plaintiffs may propose an issue class or bifurcation. *Butler* recognized that Rule 23(c)(4) is available in some circumstances, but only where the common issue is genuinely dispositive and its resolution would materially advance the case. *See* 727 F.3d at 800–02. Here, resolving the proposed common questions would leave nearly every contested issue undecided. Separate hearings on injury, causation, and amount for each member would still be needed. Defendant would also be entitled to contest each of those issues. Bifurcation would only postpone the individualized trials and would not make the class action more efficient. *See Kleen Prods. LLC v. Int'l Paper Co.*, 831 F.3d 919, 927–28 (7th Cir. 2016) (district courts must assess predominance rigorously and consider how the case will be tried). Rule 23(b)(3) does not allow certification on those terms. The Court should hold that predominance is not satisfied and deny certification.
